enc.title: Read 1.1–1.4: scales, coordinates and magnitudes

blocks.html:
• Which units make astronomical numbers manageable, and how big is each?
  • Why is the magnitude scale logarithmic and “backwards”?
Choudhuri 1.1–1.4, pp. 1–11. Look for: AU, parsec, light year, solar mass and luminosity; equatorial coordinates; apparent and absolute magnitude, the distance modulus.

Define the parsec from parallax.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>The distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsec: $d[\mathrm{pc}]=1/p[^{\prime\prime}]$, $1\,\mathrm{pc}=206265\,\mathrm{AU}=3.09\times10^{16}$ m.</details>

Two stars differ by 5 magnitudes. Flux ratio? And the distance modulus?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$m_1-m_2=-2.5\log_{10}(F_1/F_2)$: 5 mag = factor 100. $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})$ (without extinction).</details>

enc.title: Read 1.5–1.8: physics in astronomy; observing bands

blocks.html:
• What limits the sharpness of a telescope image?
  • Which wavelengths reach the ground, and why do we need space telescopes?
Choudhuri 1.5–1.8, pp. 11–22. Look for: the diffraction limit $\theta\approx1.22\lambda/D$, seeing, atmospheric windows (optical and radio), X-ray and gamma-ray astronomy from space, new messengers.

Resolution of a 10 m telescope at 500 nm vs the human eye (pupil 5 mm)?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$1.22\lambda/D=6\times10^{-8}$ rad $=0.013^{\prime\prime}$ for 10 m (in practice seeing $\sim1^{\prime\prime}$ unless adaptive optics); eye $\approx1.2\times10^{-4}$ rad $\approx25^{\prime\prime}$ (HS25 winter Q1).</details>

Why do radio interferometers reach better resolution than optical telescopes?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Resolution $\sim\lambda/B$ with the baseline $B$: intercontinental baselines (thousands of km) beat the long wavelength.</details>

enc.title: Read 2.4: stellar atmospheres and spectral lines

blocks.html:
• Why does the photosphere sit at $\tau\approx2/3$?
  • Why do absorption lines form?

Choudhuri 2.4, pp. 35–46. Look for: plane-parallel atmosphere, the grey atmosphere and Eddington approximation $T^4=\frac34T_{\rm eff}^4(\tau+\frac23)$, limb darkening, line formation from $S_\nu$ decreasing outward.

Why do absorption lines appear dark?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>At line frequencies the opacity is high, so we see shallower, cooler layers: lower $S_\nu=B_\nu(T)$ there than in the continuum.</details>
Limb darkening in the grey Eddington model?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$I(\mu)/I(1)=(3\mu+2)/5$, so $0.4$ at the limb.</details>

enc.title: Read 2.5–2.8: radiative transport inside stars; opacity; photon diffusion

blocks.html:
• How long does a photon need to get out of the Sun?
  • Which processes make stellar matter opaque?

Choudhuri 2.5–2.8, pp. 46–60. Look for: the diffusion approximation and Rosseland mean, $F\propto-\frac{1}{\kappa\rho}\frac{d(T^4)}{dr}$, Thomson scattering, Kramers law $\kappa\propto\rho T^{-7/2}$, H$^-$, the Saha equation in line analysis, the random walk out of the Sun.

Random-walk escape time from the Sun with mean free path $\ell\sim1$ cm?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$N=(R/\ell)^2$ steps, $t=N\ell/c=R^2/(\ell c)\approx(7\times10^{10}\,{\rm cm})^2/(1\,{\rm cm}\cdot3\times10^{10}\,{\rm cm/s})\approx1.6\times10^{11}$ s $\approx5000$ yr (order $10^4$ yr).</details>
Electron-scattering opacity of ionised matter?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\kappa_{\rm es}=\sigma_T(1+X)/2m_p\approx0.2(1+X)$ cm$^2$/g.</details>

enc.title: Read 3.1–3.2: equations of stellar structure

blocks.html:
• Which four equations describe a star?
  • Why does the virial theorem say a contracting star heats up?

Choudhuri 3.1–3.2, pp. 61–69. Look for: hydrostatic equilibrium, mass continuity, energy generation $dL/dr$, radiative and convective transport, the virial theorem $2K+E_G=0$, the Schwarzschild criterion.

Estimate the central pressure of the Sun from hydrostatic equilibrium.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$P_c\sim\frac{GM^2}{R^4}\approx\frac{6.7\times10^{-11}(2\times10^{30})^2}{(7\times10^8)^4}\approx10^{15}$ Pa (detailed models: $2\times10^{16}$ Pa).</details>

Virial: total energy and thermal energy of a star.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$2K=-E_G$ so $E=K+E_G=-K<0$. Losing energy (radiating) makes $E$ more negative, $K$ grows: the star contracts and heats (negative heat capacity).</details>

options: the radiative temperature gradient exceeds the adiabatic one

enc.title: Read 3.3–3.6: models, scaling relations, HR diagram, Eddington limit

blocks.html:
• Where does $L\propto M^3$ come from without solving anything?
  • What sets the upper end of the main sequence?

Choudhuri 3.3–3.6, pp. 70–90. Look for: homology and order-of-magnitude relations, $L\propto M^3$ (radiative, constant opacity), main-sequence lifetime $\propto M/L$, the HR diagram and spectral classes, cluster HR diagrams, $L_{\rm Edd}=4\pi GMc/\kappa$.

Derive $L\propto M^3$ by scaling.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$T\propto M/R$ (virial), $L\propto\frac{R^2T^4}{\kappa\rho R}\cdot R\propto\frac{R^4T^4}{\kappa M}\propto\frac{M^3}\kappa$ (radiative diffusion with $\rho\propto M/R^3$).</details>

Derive the Eddington luminosity.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Radiation force on electrons $\frac{\kappa L}{4\pi r^2c}$ per unit mass equals gravity $\frac{GM}{r^2}$: $L_{\rm Edd}=\frac{4\pi GMc}\kappa\approx1.3\times10^{31}(M/M_\odot)$ W for $\kappa_{\rm es}$ of hydrogen.</details>

enc.title: Read 4.1–4.4: nuclear reactions and the solar neutrinos

blocks.html:
• How can protons fuse at $T\sim10^7$ K when the Coulomb barrier needs $10^{10}$ K?
  • What did the solar neutrino problem teach us?

Choudhuri 4.1–4.4, pp. 91–107. Look for: tunnelling and the Gamow factor, the Gamow peak, reaction rates and their steep $T$ dependence, pp chain and CNO cycle, the binding energy per nucleon, helioseismology, solar neutrino experiments and oscillations.

Why is the reaction rate a narrow peak in energy?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Maxwell-Boltzmann tail $e^{-E/k_BT}$ times tunnelling probability $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$: the product peaks at the Gamow energy, well above $k_BT$.</details>

Why does the CNO cycle dominate in massive stars?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Its rate rises much faster with temperature ($\sim T^{16}$-$T^{20}$ vs $T^4$ for pp) because of the higher Coulomb barriers of C, N, O; hotter cores of massive stars favour it.</details>

enc.title: Read 4.5–4.9: stellar evolution, binaries, supernovae, exoplanets

blocks.html:
• What happens when hydrogen runs out in the core?
  • Which stars end as supernovae, and what is special about type Ia?

Choudhuri 4.5–4.9, pp. 108–126. Look for: post-main-sequence evolution (red giants, helium burning), binary evolution and mass transfer, mass loss, core-collapse and type Ia supernovae, rotation and magnetic fields, exoplanet detection.

Why do stars become red giants?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>The inert He core contracts and heats; H burns in a shell at higher rate, the envelope expands and cools: large radius, low $T_{\rm eff}$.</details>

Why are type Ia supernovae standard candles?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>A carbon-oxygen white dwarf near the Chandrasekhar mass ignites: similar mass, similar peak luminosity (calibrated by the decline rate).</details>

enc.title: Read 5.1–5.3: degeneracy pressure, white dwarfs, Chandrasekhar

blocks.html:
• Why does a white dwarf not collapse although it does not burn anything?
  • Why is there a maximum mass?

Choudhuri 5.1–5.3, pp. 127–136. Look for: Fermi momentum $p_F=\hbar(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$, $P\propto n^{5/3}$ (non-relativistic) and $P\propto n^{4/3}$ (relativistic), the mass-radius relation $R\propto M^{-1/3}$, the Chandrasekhar mass $\approx1.4M_\odot$.

Show that a relativistic degenerate star has no stable radius.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Degeneracy energy per electron $\sim p_Fc\propto N^{1/3}/R$, gravitational energy per nucleon $\sim-GMm_p/R$: both $\propto1/R$. Equilibrium only at one mass (Chandrasekhar); above it gravity wins at every $R$.</details>
Why does a heavier white dwarf have a smaller radius?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Non-relativistic: $P\propto\rho^{5/3}$ balanced against $GM^2/R^4$ gives $R\propto M^{-1/3}$.</details>

enc.title: Read 5.4–5.6: neutron stars, pulsars, accretion

blocks.html:
• How do neutron stars form, and how big are they?
  • Why are accreting compact objects so bright?

Choudhuri 5.4–5.6, pp. 137–152. Look for: neutron drip and inverse beta decay, neutron-star radius $\sim10$ km, pulsars as rotating magnetised neutron stars, spin-down, the binary pulsar, X-ray binaries and accretion disks.

Estimate the spin-down luminosity of a pulsar.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$L=-\frac d{dt}\frac12I\Omega^2=I\Omega|\dot\Omega|$; for the Crab $I\sim10^{38}$ kg m$^2$, $\Omega=190$ s$^{-1}$, $\dot\Omega\sim-2.4\times10^{-9}$ s$^{-2}$: $L\sim5\times10^{31}$ W, enough to power the nebula.</details>
Accretion efficiency onto a neutron star?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\eta=GM/Rc^2\approx0.2$, far above fusion (0.007).</details>

enc.title: Read 6.1–6.2: shape of the Galaxy; rotation

blocks.html:
• How did Shapley find that the Sun is not at the centre?
  • What does a flat rotation curve imply?
Choudhuri 6.1–6.2, pp. 153–165. Look for: star counts and $N(>F)\propto F^{-3/2}$, extinction and reddening, galactic coordinates, differential rotation and the Oort constants, the rotation curve.

Derive $N(>F)\propto F^{-3/2}$.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Uniform stars of luminosity $L$: those brighter than $F$ lie within $r=\sqrt{L/4\pi F}$, number $\propto r^3\propto F^{-3/2}$ (HS24 winter Q3). Deviations reveal extinction or a non-uniform distribution.</details>

Flat rotation curve $v(r)=v_0$: enclosed mass?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$M(r)=v_0^2r/G$ grows linearly with $r$, far beyond the light: dark matter halo with $\rho\propto r^{-2}$.</details>

options: extinction difference between B and V

check.explain: Dust in the disk (HS24 summer Q4).

enc.title: Read 6.3–6.4: nearly circular orbits; stellar populations

blocks.html:
• How does a star move if it is slightly off a circular orbit?
  • What distinguishes population I and II?
Choudhuri 6.3–6.4, pp. 166–174. Look for: epicycle frequency $\kappa$, solar motion and the local standard of rest, the velocity ellipsoid, populations (age, metallicity, kinematics).
Epicycle frequency for a flat rotation curve?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\kappa^2=R\frac{d\Omega^2}{dR}+4\Omega^2$; with $\Omega=v_0/R$: $\kappa=\sqrt2\Omega$.</details>

Population II stars: where and why?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Halo and globular clusters: old, metal-poor (formed before the ISM was enriched), with large random velocities and slow rotation.</details>

enc.title: Read 6.5–6.6: the interstellar gas and its phases

blocks.html:
• How do we see cold hydrogen at all?
  • Why is the ISM in several phases at roughly equal pressure?
Choudhuri 6.5–6.6, pp. 174–187. Look for: the 21 cm line, HI clouds, warm intercloud medium, molecular clouds and CO, HII regions and the Strömgren sphere, hot coronal gas.

Strömgren radius of an O star emitting $Q$ ionising photons per second in gas of density $n$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Ionisations balance recombinations: $Q=\frac43\pi R_S^3n^2\alpha_B$, so $R_S=\left(\frac{3Q}{4\pi n^2\alpha_B}\right)^{1/3}$ (HS25 practice Q4).</details>

Why is the 21 cm line so useful despite its tiny transition probability?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>The Galaxy holds so much HI that the line is bright; radio waves pass dust, and Doppler shifts give the rotation curve.</details>

options: the hyperfine spin flip of hydrogen

enc.title: Read 6.7–6.8: magnetic field, cosmic rays, thermal balance of the ISM

blocks.html:
• How is the galactic magnetic field measured?
  • What heats and cools the ISM?
Choudhuri 6.7–6.8, pp. 187–196. Look for: Faraday rotation and Zeeman splitting, cosmic rays and their spectrum, heating by UV and cosmic rays, cooling functions, pressure equilibrium of the phases.

How does Faraday rotation measure $B$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>The polarisation angle rotates as $\lambda^2\cdot$RM with $\mathrm{RM}\propto\int n_eB_\parallel ds$; combined with the dispersion measure $\int n_eds$ of pulsars gives $\langle B_\parallel\rangle\sim$ few $\mu$G.</details>

enc.title: Read 7.1–7.4: virial theorem, relaxation, self-gravity

blocks.html:
• When do star-star encounters matter in a galaxy?
  • Why can a self-gravitating system never reach thermal equilibrium?

Choudhuri 7.1–7.4, pp. 197–206. Look for: the virial theorem for stellar systems, two-body relaxation time $t_{\rm relax}\approx\frac N{8\ln N}t_{\rm cross}$, negative heat capacity, the isothermal sphere’s infinite mass.

Relaxation time of a galaxy with $N=10^{11}$, $t_{\rm cross}=10^8$ yr?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\frac{10^{11}}{8\cdot25}\cdot10^8\approx5\times10^{16}$ yr $\gg$ the age of the Universe: galaxies are collisionless; globular clusters ($N\sim10^5$) are not.</details>

Virial mass of a cluster with velocity dispersion $\sigma$ and radius $R$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$M\sim\frac{\sigma^2R}G$ (factor of order unity from the profile): the classic evidence for dark matter in clusters (HS25 practice Q5).</details>

enc.title: Read 7.5–7.7: collisionless Boltzmann and Jeans equations

blocks.html:
• How do you describe $10^{11}$ stars without following each one?
  • What do the Jeans equations let you measure?

Choudhuri 7.5–7.7, pp. 207–218. Look for: the distribution function and the collisionless Boltzmann equation, velocity moments giving the Jeans equations, the Oort limit, asymmetric drift, the two subsystems of solar-neighbourhood stars.

enc.title: Read 8.2–8.3: fluid equations and the Jeans instability

blocks.html:
• When does a gas cloud collapse under its own weight?
  • What competes with gravity?
Choudhuri 8.2–8.3, pp. 220–227. Look for: continuity and Euler equations, linear perturbations, the dispersion relation $\omega^2=c_s^2k^2-4\pi G\rho_0$, the Jeans length and mass.

Derive the Jeans length from the dispersion relation.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Instability for $\omega^2<0$: $k<k_J=\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0}/c_s$, so $\lambda_J=c_s\sqrt{\pi/(G\rho_0)}$ and $M_J\sim\rho_0\lambda_J^3$.</details>

Why do cold, dense molecular clouds form stars?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$M_J\propto T^{3/2}\rho^{-1/2}$: low $T$ and high $\rho$ make the Jeans mass small, so ordinary clouds exceed it.</details>

enc.title: Read 9.1–9.2: normal galaxies

blocks.html:
• How are galaxies classified, and does the classification mean evolution?
  • What do Tully-Fisher and Faber-Jackson relate?

Choudhuri 9.1–9.2, pp. 261–270. Look for: the Hubble sequence (ellipticals, spirals, irregulars), surface-brightness profiles (de Vaucouleurs, exponential disks), rotation curves, Tully-Fisher $L\propto v^4$, Faber-Jackson $L\propto\sigma^4$, open questions.
Why can Tully-Fisher be used as a distance indicator?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Measure $v_{\max}$ (21 cm line width), infer $L\propto v^4$, compare with the flux: distance.</details>

Spiral vs elliptical: list three physical differences.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Spirals: rotation-supported disk, gas and young stars, blue. Ellipticals: dispersion-supported, little cold gas, old red stars (HS24 winter Q5).</details>

enc.title: Read 9.4: active galactic nuclei

blocks.html:
• What powers a quasar, and how do we know the engine is small?
  • Why do AGN types differ if the engine is the same?

Choudhuri 9.4, pp. 276–285. Look for: the AGN zoo, variability and the size limit $R\lesssim c\Delta t$, superluminal motion, black-hole accretion as the engine (Eddington), unification by viewing angle.

A quasar varies in 1 day. Size limit and black-hole bound?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$R\lesssim c\Delta t\approx2.6\times10^{13}$ m $\approx170$ AU; with $R\gtrsim R_S=2GM/c^2$: $M\lesssim\frac{c^3\Delta t}{2G}\approx10^{10}M_\odot$ (HS24 winter Q6).</details>
Minimum black-hole mass for $L=10^{40}$ W at the Eddington limit?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$M\ge L/(1.3\times10^{31}\,{\rm W}/M_\odot)\approx8\times10^8M_\odot$.</details>

blocks.html:
• Which three ways to weigh a cluster agree that most of its mass is dark?
  • How is the hot gas in clusters seen?
Choudhuri 9.5–9.7, pp. 286–296. Look for: virial masses, X-ray gas and hydrostatic masses, gravitational lensing, the large-scale distribution of galaxies, gamma-ray bursts.

Cluster X-ray luminosity from bremsstrahlung: scaling?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$L_X\propto n_e^2T^{1/2}V$; with the virial temperature $k_BT\sim GMm_p/R$, $L_X$ grows steeply with mass (HS25 winter Q5).</details>

enc.title: Read 9.3: the expansion of the Universe

blocks.html:
• How do you measure distances to galaxies, and what did Hubble find?
  • Why is redshift not a Doppler velocity at large distance?
Choudhuri 9.3, pp. 271–275. Look for: the distance ladder (parallax, Cepheids, standard candles), redshift $z$, Hubble’s law $v=H_0d$, the Hubble time.
Hubble time for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$1/H_0=\frac{3.09\times10^{19}\,{\rm km}}{70\,{\rm km/s}}=4.4\times10^{17}$ s $\approx14$ Gyr.</details>

enc.title: Read 10.1–10.4: metric of the Universe and the Friedmann equation

blocks.html:
• What does homogeneity and isotropy fix about the metric?
  • Which quantities enter the Friedmann equation?

Choudhuri 10.1–10.4, pp. 297–312. Look for: basic GR ideas, the Robertson-Walker metric with $a(t)$ and $k$, comoving coordinates and redshift $1+z=a_0/a$, the Friedmann equation $\dot a^2/a^2=\frac{8\pi G}3\rho-\frac{kc^2}{a^2}$ (with $\Lambda$), critical density.
Critical density today for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\rho_c=\frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}\approx9.2\times10^{-27}$ kg/m$^3$, about 5 protons per m$^3$.</details>

Derive the Newtonian Friedmann equation.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Shell of radius $R=ar$ around mass $M=\frac43\pi R^3\rho$: energy $\frac12\dot R^2-\frac{GM}R=$ const. Divide by $R^2/2$: $\frac{\dot a^2}{a^2}=\frac{8\pi G\rho}3-\frac{kc^2}{a^2}$.</details>

enc.title: Read 10.5–10.7: contents, CMB, matter and radiation eras

blocks.html:
• How does each component dilute as the Universe expands?
  • Why was the early Universe radiation dominated?

Choudhuri 10.5–10.7, pp. 313–324. Look for: $\rho_m\propto a^{-3}$, $\rho_r\propto a^{-4}$, $T\propto1/a$, the CMB blackbody at 2.7 K, closed and open matter solutions, the age, $a\propto t^{2/3}$ (matter) and $a\propto t^{1/2}$ (radiation).

Solve the flat matter-dominated Friedmann equation.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\dot a^2\propto a^{-1}$: $a^{1/2}da\propto dt$, $a\propto t^{2/3}$, $H=\frac2{3t}$, age $t_0=\frac2{3H_0}$.</details>

Generalise: $\rho\propto a^{-3(1+w)}$ in a flat universe.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$a\propto t^{2/(3(1+w))}$: $w=0$ gives $\frac23$, $w=\frac13$ gives $\frac12$ (HS24 summer Q7).</details>

Choudhuri 11.1–11.4, pp. 325–335. Look for: the time table, $T\propto t^{-1/2}$, thermal equilibrium and relativistic degrees of freedom, neutron-proton freeze-out, BBN and the helium mass fraction, the neutrino background $T_\nu=(4/11)^{1/3}T_\gamma$.
Helium fraction from $n/p\approx1/7$ at nucleosynthesis?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>All neutrons end in $^4$He: $Y=\frac{2(n/p)}{1+n/p}=\frac{2/7}{8/7}=0.25$.</details>

Why is the neutrino background colder than the CMB?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Neutrinos decouple before $e^+e^-$ annihilation, which heats only the photons: $T_\nu/T_\gamma=(4/11)^{1/3}\approx0.71$, $T_\nu\approx1.95$ K.</details>

• What is the CMB a picture of, and when?
  • How did small fluctuations grow into galaxies?

Choudhuri 11.5–11.9, pp. 336–356. Look for: hot vs cold dark matter, the horizon problem and inflation, baryogenesis, recombination and last scattering at $z\approx1100$, CMB anisotropies, the SZ effect, the Ly$\alpha$ forest, growth of perturbations.

Why does recombination happen at $T\approx3000$ K and not at 13.6 eV $\approx1.6\times10^5$ K?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>There are $\sim10^9$ photons per baryon: even at $k_BT\ll13.6$ eV the Wien tail holds enough ionising photons until $T\approx3000$ K ($z\approx1100$).</details>

Why must most dark matter be cold?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Hot (relativistic) dark matter free-streams and erases small-scale structure (top-down); observed hierarchical (bottom-up) formation needs cold dark matter.</details>
